Completion of irrigation projects 
40l. DR. D. MASTHAN: 
SHRI RAJIV RANJAN SINGH:+ + 
Will the Minister of WATER RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the construction on a number of irrigation projects is 
going on in order to complete them during the Ninth Five Year Plan; 
(b) if so, the State-wise names of those irrigation projects in the country which are 
to be completed during the Ninth Five Year Plan; and 
(c) the total amount of funds allocated for their construction; and the amount 
actually spent on each of the above projects till March, 2000? 
THE MINISTER OF WATER RESOURCES (SHRI ARJUN SETHI): (a) to (c) A 
Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) to (c) Statewise details of 162 major and 240 medium ongoing irrigation projects 
which have spilled over into IX Plan alongwith their latest estimated cost expenditure 
upto the end of VIII Plan and spillover cost in IX Plan are given, in the enclosed table 
(See below). Of these 7 major and 6 medium projects have already been completed. 
The Completion of any other project during the balance period of IX Plan depends on 
various factors such as its size, acquisition of  land, forest clearance, rehabilitation and 
resettlement, geological conditions etc. Equally important are availability and 
allocation of funds by the State Governments to individual projects. 
Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
The question was actually asked on the floor of the House by Shri Rajiv Ranjan 
Singh..

SHRI ARJUN SETHI: Sir, the hon. Member has asked about the slow progress of 
various irrigation projects in the State of Bi har. The hon. Member will appreciate that, 
irrigation being a State subject, the Ministry of Water Resources at the Centre can only 
monitor. The implementation, execution as also the funding of the projects are being 
done by the State Governments. For the completion of the ongoing projects we 
provide Central Loan Assistance to the Stat e Governments, and the projects, which 
they want to take up, are recommended by the State Governments concerned. The hon. 
Member will appreciate that we arc doing whatever is possible. We can monitor the 
projects. But the execution and the implementation are in the hands of the States 
concerned. So, I am afraid, as the Water Resources Minister at the Centre, I cannot 
give any direction

to the State Governments or supervise the implementation of the projects. They decide 
the priorities and implement the projects as per their own decision. 
SHRI RAJIV RANJAN SINGH: What is the reason? 
SHRI ARJUN SETHI: Sir, the main reas on is paucity of funds. Sometimes, the 
State Governments take up many projects at a time. As a result, the funds available 
are inadequate to complete the ongoing projects.

The telecom facilities in rural areas have progressed considerably over the last few 
years. Presently, Department of Telecom Operations is operating 2,74,20,192 Direct 
Exchange Lines (DELs) in the country out of which 49,26,287 DELs are working in 
rural areas. This is being done through 28,204 telephone exchanges in the country out 
of which 21,879 are in rural areas. In addition, out of 6.07 lakh villages, Public 
Telephones have been provided in 3,76,886 villages. It is further planned to provide a 
total of 57.9 lakh lines in the country (i ncluding MTNL) in the current financial year 
2000-2001, out of which 14.2 lakh lines will be in rural areas through the existing 
exchanges in rural areas as well as 3,431 new exchanges planned for opening in rural 
areas. It is also planned to provide 19 lakh lines in rural areas during 2001-2002. 
The Government has decided as a policy, to make available Telephone on Demand 
by the end of Ninth Five Year Plan in the entire country which includes both rural as 
well as urban areas along with the contribution of private sector. The Government has 
also envisaged that all the exchanges in the country will be covered with reliable 
transmission media by the end of Ninth Plan. The New Telecom Policy—1999 also 
envisages that each village in the country will have at least one Public Telephone by 
the end of Ninth Five Year Plan along with the contribution from Private Sector. All 
out efforts are being made to achieve these targets.

Nitrates and Flouride in Ground Water of Delhi 
*408.  SHRI PREM CHAND GUPTA: SHRI 
SANJAY NIRUPAM: 
Will the Minister of WATER RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
 whether it is a fact that TERI has repo rted that the ground water in Delhi 
contains dangerously high quantities of Nitrates and Flouride which is harmful to 
health; and 
 if so, what action Government are taking to protect the people from this 
hazard? 
THE MINISTER OF WATER RESOURCES (SHRI ARJUN SETHI): (a) and (b) The 
Tata Energy and Research Institute (TERI) have not reported that "ground water in 
Delhi contains dangerously high quantities of nitrate and flouride which is harmful to 
health". However, a joint study made by the Central Ground Water Board (CGWB) 
and the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) have reported the presence of high 
quantities of flouride and nitrate in ground water of some parts of Alipur, Kanjhawala, 
Najafgarh, Shahdara and city blocks of Delhi. 
Water being a State subject, provision of drinking water supply is the responsibility 
of the State Governments. The Rajiv Gandhi National Drinking Water Mission has 
however been assisting and guiding the States in providing safe drinking water to rural 
areas under the Accelerated Rural Water Supply Programme and exclusive sub-
mission programmes in areas having serious ground wa ter quality problems like 
flouride, iron arsenic and brackishness. In su ch areas where ground water is unfit for 
drinking, safe drinking water is provided through alternative sources, either by tapping 
surface water or by undertaking remedial measures like deflouridation, iron and 
arsenic removal. A total of 632 defluoridation plants, 150 desalination plants and 9524 
iron removal plants have been installed at different places in various States. 
The steps taken by the Union Government and the Delhi Jal Board to protect the 
people from this hazard include: 
(i) The Delhi Jal Board produces about 640 Million Gallon/Day (MGD) water. Out 
of this 72 MGD (11.25%) is ground water 
32 

[22 August, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
and the remaining 568 MGD (88.75%) is surface water. The surface water is treated 
in modern treatment plants. Out of 72 MDG ground water, 6 MGD water is treated at 
an ozonisation and nitrification plant at Okhla in South Delhi and the rest is supplied 
after chlorination. 
(ii) Works of rain water harvesting/recharging of aquifer have been taken up by the 
Delhi Jal Board individually and also through the Resident Welfare 
Associations under Bhagidari Scheme. The Delhi Jal Board has taken up 65 
such projects. 
(iii) The project of prevention and control of fluorosis has been  launched by the 
Delhi Government's Health Department. 
(iv) A 40 MDG water treatment plant has recently been commissioned at Nangloi 
and a 20 MDG plant is nearing completion at Bawana. These plants shall 
draw raw water from surface sources only for treatment. 
(v) The Central Ground Water Authority has declared Najafgarh and Mehrauli 
blocks of Delhi as notified areas for control and regulated development of 
ground water. 
(vi) The Delhi Jal Board has identified hand pumps and other structures in polluted 
areas where the shallow ground water is not fit for human consumption and 
painted them red with warning. 
(vii) The Central Ground Water Authority has organised mass awareness 
programmes among the public, indus trialists and industrial workers 
regarding pollution and over-extraction of ground water. 
(viii) The Central Ground Water Board is periodically monitoring water quality for 
the NCT Delhi.

416. SHRI C. RAMACHANDRAIAH: Will the Minister of FINANCE be pleased 
to state: 
 the approximate amount of income tax paid in the normal course every month 
by Government officials of the rank of section officer and above; 
 whether it is a fact that incidence of income tax is harsh in cases of single 
incomes and for planning post retirement requirements; 
 the steps Government propose to rationalise the income tax structure to 
provide for zero tax liability by promoting short and long term savings in priority 
sectors; and 
 whether Government propose to withdraw the surcharge on income tax as 
promised by the Finance Minister at the time  of its imposition, if so, by when; and if 
not the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (V. 
DHANANJAY KUMAR): (a) No such statistics  are maintained in respect of the 
amount of income-tax paid every month by Government Officials of any particular 
cadre. 
(b) In view of the threshold limit of Income-tax of Rs. 50,000/- for individuals, 
standard deduction on salaried income upto a maximum amount of Rs. 25,000/- and 
maximum tax rebate of Rs. 16,000/- on 
40 

[22 August, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
specified savings, and taking into account other deductions and exemptions, the 
incidence of income-tax cannot be said to be harsh on any class of tax payers. 
Besides, there are specific schemes exempting income of certain classes of 
employment. Interest income on notified bonds or debentures is exempt under section 
10(15) of the Income-tax Act. 
(c) To rationalise the income-tax  structure, the Government 
reviews saving schemes provided for priority sectors during the 
annual budget exercise. Some of the steps taken to provide short and 
long term savings in priority sectors, include tax rebate under 
Section-88 for investments in equity shares or bonds made by a public 
company developing infrastructure facility. Under Section 54EC, long 
term capital gains becomes tax free if invested in bonds issued by 
National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development and National 
Highways Authority of India. 
(d) The surcharge of Income-tax is levied on an yearly basis and 
only when necessitated by unavoidable circumstances. An across-the- 
board 10% surcharge was levied through Finance Act, 1999 to cater 
to growing development expenditure and also to contain the revenue 
and fiscal deficit. The surcharge was meant to be temporary but had 
to be continued next year due to a heavy and unexpected expenditure 
burden, mainly on account of defence requirements and transfer to 
States mandated by the Finance Commission. The rate of surcharge 
was moderately increased from 10% to 15% on non-corporate 
taxpayers in the Finance Act, 2000. 
As per the provisions of the Act, the surcharge will lapse after the financial year 
ends. Whether the same is to be re-introduced or not, will be considered at the time of 
preparation of next budget and will depend  on the expenditure requirements of the

World Bank report on strengthening of TRAI 
3142. SHRI R. P. GOENKA: Will the Minister of COMMUNICATIONS be 
pleased to state: 
 whether the World Bank in its Country Framework Report has called for the 
strengthening of the TRAFs powers to reduce the likelihood of conflict of interests in 
the telecom sector; 
 if so, the fresh initiatives contemplated in the matter; and 
 the other major recommendations/observations relating to the Ministry made 
by the World Bank recently and the action taken thereon?

(SHRI TAPAN SIKDAR): (a) Yes, Sir.

legislative amendments to the TRAI Act of 1997 so as to remove the 
ambiguities and difficulties that had arisen in the implementation of 
the TRAI Act, strengthen the regulatory framework and strengthen 
the disputes settlement mechanism. Thus these amendments have 
significantly strengthened the role of the regulator.

telecommunications markets, clarifyi ng universal service obligations 
and efficient allocation of the spectrum. The issues are broadly 
governed by New Telecom Policy, 1999 and actions have been 
initiated accordingly. These include de-regulation of national long 
distance services without any restriction on number of licences to be 
issued subject to the Licencees paying a stipulated entry fee and a 
share of revenues, migration of existing licence holders to a revenue 
sharing regime and initiating the process of the introduction of new 
entrants to cellular services in consultation with TRAI, initiating 
consultation with TRAI in matte rs concerning universal service 
obligations and development of National Frequency Allocation Plan,

Settlement of river water disputes 
3248. SHRI NARENDRA MOHAN: Will the Minister of WATER RESOURCES 
be pleased to state: 
 whether under the Water Dispute Act 1956, four or five tribunals were set up 
to settle water disputes of rivers like Godavari, Narmada, Krishna, Ravi, Beas and 
Kaveri etc.; 
 what is the progress of settlement about these disputes; and 
 what problems are being faced in this regard and details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER RESOURCES 
(SHRIMATI BIJOYA CHAKRAVARTY): (a) to (c) 
Godavari, Narmada and Krishna water disputes relating to sharing of waters of these 
rivers were referred to the tribunals under Inter State Water Disputes Act, 1956 in 
1969. The Tribunals have submitted the final report to Central Government in 1980, 
1979 and. 1976 respectively. Ravi and Beas water dispute and Cauvery water disputes 
were referred to the Tribunal, under the provisions of the said Act for adjudication in 
April, 1986 and June, 1990 respectively. Ravi and Beas Water Tribunal has submitted 
its report on 30.1.1987. The Central Government as well as the party States of 
Rajasthan, Haryana and Punjab have sought explanation and guidance on certain points 
from the Tribunal under Section 5(3) of the Inter-State Water Disputes Act, 1956. 
Cauvery Water Disputes Tribunal passed an interim order oh June 25, 1991 giving 
relief to State of Tamil Nadu and Union Territory of Pondicherry. The Central 
Government has published the interim order in the official gazette on 10.12.91 making 
it final and binding on the parties to the disputes. In pursuance of order of the 
Supreme Court dated 9.4.1997, the Central Government has framed a scheme under 
Section 6A of the said Act for giving effect to the interim order and all its related 
subsequent orders. The scheme consists of the Cauvery River Authority headed by the 
Prime Minister with the Chief Ministers of the basin States as its members. The 
Authority is assisted by a Monitoring Committee headed by the Secretary (Water 
Resources).

India has been fighting efforts to patent inherently traditional items like 
neem, karela, basmati, etc. Now, it seems th at the spiritual heritage of meditation like

SHRI K. RAMA MOHANA RAO (Andhra Pradesh): Sir, my Special 
Mention pertains to the shortage of pilots and commanders in Indian Airlines. The 
sudden change in the policy of the IA, of rolling back the retirement age of its

commanders who retired, four were trainers and examiners. The important point is, in

pilots in the coming five years, at the rate of 4 sets of crew for each aircraft. The 
commanders who retired did not return to the IA for contractual appointment. I 
understand that majority of them have gone to private airlines because the private 
airlines give them attractive perks and other benefits. The retirement has brought about 
a strain on airlines' operations, particularly Airbps-300. There is also a proposal before 
the I.A. to dry lease about six A-320s within this year. Keeping all these things in 
view, the IA need more pilots, but the surpri sing thing is, there has not been a single 
appointment in the IA for the last eight years.  Even if a new pilot joins the IA, it will 
take a minimum of two years for him to become a full-fledged pilot. I do not know 
what the Ministry is doing with regard to recruiting pilots. I think, there are about 20 
pilots on deputation with Alliance Air; and I do not know whether there is any 
thinking going on in the Ministry to recall them to their parent organisation.

I stand to support the Bill. The Bill makes two small amendments which are 
for the benefit of the workmen. Therefore, they are welcome. Employment of a casual 
nature is now covered. And there is a marginal increase in the pecuniary limit. So far, 
so good. Therefore, I compliment the hon. Minister for bringing this measure. But I 
believe that much remains to be done in th is behalf. Strangely, while including those 
persons whose employment is of a casual nature and who are employed otherwise 
than for purposes of the employer's trade or business, Schedule II of the Act excludes 
those who are working in a clerical capacity. In fact, if casual employment is also 
covered by the Act, it is all the more necessary that the employment of those who are 
working in a clerical capacity should also be covered. The crux of the matter, insofar 
as workmen's compensation is concerned, is the injury which arises out of and during 
the course of employment. And a clerk, as every other worker, is in the place where he 
meets with the accident because of his employment. The age-old test laid down by 
Justice Chagte is, "Why was he there? He was there only because of his employment. 
And therefore, he is entitled to compensation." That equally applies to clerks, and 
therefore, they should also be covered by this

benefit of compensation. I may mention that in a comparable enactment, namely, the 
ESI Act, clerks are covered, and there is no reason why they are not covered by the 
Workmen's Compensation Act. I have another suggestion to make in so far as the 
amount of compensation that is made payable is concerned. The computation of the 
compensation under section 4, read with Schedule 4, is done in a manner which is not 
intelligible to common man, maybe, sometimes, to the lawyers, because an acturial 
method is employed and a smaller figure is ultimately computed even though the 
workman is getting a salary of a proportionately higher range. So, the increase of the 
limit to Rs. 4,000/- is, as a matter of fact, ridiculous, looking to the value of the rupee 
which it has attained during the last few year s, and therefore, it will be reasonable if 
the compensation is based on the emoluments of the employee, without depending 
upon the higher limit, and whatever the emoluments, the compensation should be 
commensurate to those emoluments. I have mentioned already that the aspect of 
computation is unintelligible, and that so metimes brings injustice to the workman 
concerned. 
There is a third aspect to which I would like to draw the attention both of the 
House and the Minister, and it is regarding the list of occupational diseases in the 
enactment. This list today is thoroughly outdated, particularly in view of the fact that 
the increase in the industries with chemicals is enormous, and in fact, because of 
several international conventions, the Factories Act has been amended to introduce a 
substantial chapter to cover hazardous substances and safety measures in so far as the 
workmen are concerned. In fact, the rules under the Act make it mandatory for the 
employer to subject his employees to medical examination every six months. The 
diseases that one gets afflicted with because of his exposure to various hazardous 
substances and chemicals, are not covered by the Act, because the diseases which 
were considered occupational almost a century ago, even though the enactment is of 
1923, are only the diseases covered by the enactment. Therefore, the Schedule in 
respect of occupational diseases which is thoroughly outdated, ought to be replaced, to 
include diseases for which protection is sought by express provisions under the 
Factories Act. 
Lastly, I would submit that the definition of compensation should also be 
reviewed. Today, an employee is entitled to compensation as provided by an 
enactment. But we have industries where trade unions are strong and they enter into 
agreements providing for higher compensation.

that. Therefore, the definition of compensation which is now only that which is

parties, naturally whichever is higher. I, therefore, submit that even though this Bill is 
meant for the benefit of the employees, it does its job only marginally in so far as the 
diseases covered, in so far as the employees , including clerks covered are concerned.

Madam Deputy Chairperson, the Workmen's Compensation (Amendment) 
Bill needs a thorough and detailed revision. The reasons for demanding  such  a 
revision are  many.     Take,  for example,  the  list  of 
243 

RAJYA SABHA [22 August, 2000] 
occupational diseases, which is given in the Schedule of the Act. The Member who 
spoke earlier has stated that it is almost outmoded. When newer and newer industries 
have come into being, new methods of production, new methods of operation, new 
products are being introduced. Several types of energy are being used. Several types of 
equipment are being employed in industry and trade. Several diseases-heart problems, 
bone-related diseases, damages to eyes and brain, skin diseases-are reported to be 
connected with occupational hazards. The list of occupational hazards does not 
consider these diseases; that list is outmoded outright. These things should be 
examined thoroughly, and an amendment to the Act should be brought in. That is point 
number one I want to say. 
The minimum amount of compensation has been increased. It is welcome. 
But it is inadequate. In the case of fatal accidents, for permanent disablement, an 
amount of Rs.90,000/- is being fixed as compensation. It is totally inadequate. It 
should be a minimum of Rs.1.5 lakhs. Not only that; for permanent total disablement, 
a worker who is affected by an accident should be given pension till his death. Not 
only that; the next of kin or dependent should be given employment in the industry 
where the employee works and meets with an accident. 
The expenditure for funeral has also been increased. But nowadays, the 
amount, taking into consideration the expenses of funeral, should be enhanced to at 
least Rs. 10,000/-. 
There is a very good suggestion to include casual and temporary workers to 
be benefited by the Workmen's Compensation Act. It is welcome. But I demand that 
every worker, whether he is a clerk or a supervisor or a manager, should be covered 
by the Act, and the benefit should be awarded to him. 
The third point which I want to stress is that in factories and industrial 
establishments, the precaution taken for prevention of accidents is totally inadequate. 
The Factories Act and many other labour laws have some provisions regarding the 
safety of workers, but the managements gi ve only low priority to those rules and 
regulations. It should be thoroughly examined, and a proper legislation should be 
brought. That is my third point. 
244 

[22 August, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
Lastly, I would like to stress that the workers, who are handling these 
products and machines and transporting these goods, should be given training on how 
to deal with them. Many poisonous, inflammable, explosive and dangerous substances 
are transported by rail, road and other modes of transport. Many accidents are taking 
place. Not only the workers but the general public also are affected by these accidents. 
How do we deal with the situation? The workers should be thoroughly trained in 
dealing with these things. Proper instructions should be displayed on the vehicles that 
carry such explosive substances. This type of amendments should be made to the 
Workmen's Compensation Act. Then only can the accidents be prevented. Measures 
capable of preventing accidents should be taken and implemented properly. 
While supporting the Bill, I request the hon. Minister to come forward with 
a comprehensive amendment to the Workmen's Compensation Act. Thank you.

SHRI H.K. JAVARE GOWDA (Karnataka): Madam, I welcome the 
Workmen's Compensation (Amendment) Bill, 2000. The amendments proposed to 
section 2, covering casual employees, and also section 4, enhancing the compensation, 
in case of death from Rs. 50,000 to Rs. 80,000 and, in case of disability, from Rs. 
60,000 to Rs. 90,000, are welcome. 
Also, the proposed new sub-section (3A) of section 4A says, "The interest 
and the penalty payable under sub-section (3) shall be paid to the workman...." 
Madam, in the case of death of a person, the quantum of compensation is very, very 
low. It will not be enough for the dependents of the deceased. Then, in the case of a 
disabled man, the enhanced amount is fixed at roughly Rs. 90,000. But it does not 
include the medical expenditure. In many cases of injury, it has been seen that the 
medical expenditure goes up to Rs. 1,00,000; Rs.1,50,000; or even up to Rs. 2,00,000. 
It depends on the nature of the injury; not on the employment. Under such 
circumstances, a special provision or a clause should be inserted stating that, apart 
from the compensation of Rs. 90,000, the medical expenditure will also have to be 
paid by the insurance company or the employer; otherwise, this Act will not serve its 
purpose. As a legislative authority, we owe a responsibility to incl ude that aspect of 
the matter in this Act. 
My next point which needs to be taken into consideration is regarding the 
mode of payment of the interest and the penalty.   In almost
